title: Multiplexed back focal plane imaging with on-chip integrated microlens array

paper_content.abstract: On-chip optical architectures that enable angle-resolved spectroscopy are essential for advancing photonic platforms towards low-volume, scalable, and cryo-compatible devices. Here, we introduce spatially resolved momentum-space imaging using arrays of 3D-printed microlenses directly integrated onto semiconductor optical microcavities. Each microlens functions as an independent optical element with a high numerical aperture (approx.0.95),enablingparallelbackfocalplaneimagingacross,inourimplementation,64distinctlocations.Thisapproach eliminates the need for bulky microscope objectives while maintaining broad wavevector access, even undercryogenicconditions. ThemicrolensesnotonlyenhancEecollectionefficiencybutalsoenabletightlyfocusedexcitation,yieldinganorderofmagnitudereductionincondensationthresholdscomparedwithconventional setups. Our results establish 3D-printed microlens arrays as a compact, versatile, integrated platform for next-generationangle-resolvedspectroscopyinnanophotonicsPandquantummaterials.
paper_content.introduction:
Back focal plane (BFP) imaging, also referred to as reciprocalspace,k-space,orFourierplaneimaging,isa widelyusedexperimentaltechniquethatmLapstheangular distribution of light emitted or transmitted by a sample.Inmanyopticalandphotonicsystems,thisangle is directly linked to the in-planewavevector (momentum)oflightorquasiparticleTexcitations.

As such, momentum-resolved spectroscopy offers direct insights in all subfields of photonics1,2. Yet, accessing momentum-space typically relies on bulky microscope objectives that limit experimental flexibility, especially under cryogenic conditions or in scalable device geometries. On-chip optical elements offer a pathway toward compact and integrable solutions,wherelightcanbecollected,focused,andmanipulateddirectlyatthedevicelevel. Inparticular,three-dimensionalprintingofmicroopticalcomponentsprovides remarkable freedom to design monolithic architectureswithsite-specificfunctionality.

In nanophotonics and plasmonics, the directionalityoflightpropagationplaysanessentialrole. There, BFP imaging has been adapted to investigate various devicessuchasplasmonicnanowires3,4 ornanoantennas5–7, as well as diverse optical phenomena such as surface-enhancedRamanscattering8,secondandthird harmonicgeneration9,10,cathodoluminescence11,12,and up-conversion13. Thetechniquehasalsoprovenvaluableinthequantumregime14–16, whereitprovidesaccesstotheangularemissioncharacteristicsofquantum emitters.

On the fundamental level, BFP imaging allows to determine the direction of a dipole transition, such as identifying the orientation of single molecules17,18 or carbonnanotubes19.Thesamemethodhasbeenusedto distinguishthein-planeorout-of-planecharacterofexcitonsinlayeredmaterials20,21, theirheterostructures22 andthinorganicfilmsinOLEDs23.Italsoallowstodifferentiate from the most common electric-dipole transitions scarce magnetic-dipole ones, occurring in rare earthscomplexes24orin2Dperovskites25.

In systems such as photonic crystals, nanostructures, metasurfaces, or optical cavities, the wavelength and wavevector of photons are connected, forming intricate energy-momentum dispersion relations. There, momentum-resolved spectroscopy enables the experimental study of a wide range of physical phenomena originating from the specific structure in momentum-space. Thisincludestopologicalstates,suchasbound states in the continuum26,27, topologically protected edgemodes28–30, andphotonicanaloguesofelectronic topological insulators31,32. It also allows exploration of solid-state analogies, including photonic lattices33, Dirac cones34, and Berry curvature-related phenomena35–37. Furthermore, this approach provides access tonon-Hermitianphysics,suchasmanipulationofexceptional points38,39, or optical simulations of exotic physics far from classical optics, such as analogues of blackholehorizons40,41andnewphasesofmatter42.

Conventional approaches to reciprocal space imaging rely on high-magnification, high-numerical-aperture(NA)microscopeobjectivestoaccessabroad angle range, often spanning several tens of degrees. These same objectives are typically used for excitation, as their large NA enables the tight focusing requiredtoachievethehighpowerdensitiesnecessary for reaching nonlinear phenomena. However, these optical elements come with significant limitations. Their short working distances make integration with cryogenicsystemsparticularlychallenging. Moreover, they inherently restrict measurements to a single spatial location at a time, since they integrate angular informationovertheentirecollectionarea. Asaresult, conventionalexcitationanddetectionschemeslackthe capability for spatially multiplexed momentum-space imaging,limitingexperimentalaccesstonon-localphenomena.Thisprecludesstudiesofspatiallydistributed momentum-space dynamics and related phenomena suchasJosephsonoscillations,site-to-sitecouplings,or momentum-dependent particle population, flow, and thermalization.

Here,wepresentaphotonicapproachbasedonellipsoidalmicrolensesdirectlyprintedontopofopticalmicrocavities, replacingtheconventionalmicroscopeobjectiveinboththeexcitationanddetectionpaths. This allows for simultaneous momentum-space imaging of multiple (up to 64) spatial positions, each with access to large emission angles (up to 72 degrees in air, NA = 0.95), all while eliminating the need for bulky microscope objectives. The high NA of microlenses also provides tight focusing of the excitation beam, which significantly reduces the threshold of polariton Bose-Einsteincondensationbynearlyanorderofmagnitude compared to conventional microscope objective excitation. The versatility and robustness of printed microlensesisdemonstratedinbothpurelyphotonicand exciton-polaritonopticalmicrocavities.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Furman et al. present an integration of 3D-printed ellipsoidal microlens arrays directly onto optical microcavities for multiplexed, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The approach successfully replaces bulky microscope objectives with integrated on-chip optics, achieving broad numerical aperture access (up to NA ≈ 0.95) even under cryogenic conditions. The demonstration of 64-site simultaneous k-space imaging represents a genuine breakthrough in experimental methodology. However, a number of conceptual and technical aspects require clarification. These include a fuller quantification of strain-induced effects, explicit comparison of wavevector resolution trade-offs, and a stronger substantiation of the claimed dynamic multiplexing capabilities.
Below are some comments for the author’s consideration.
1. The 3D-printed polymer microlenses introduce localized strain on the semiconductor surface, leading to measurable blueshifts of the exciton and cavity resonances. Given that this strain can affect local mode energies and potentially distort comparisons across the microlens array, its influence requires deeper quantification. The current acknowledgment of this effect in the text is insufficient for reproducibility. The authors should include a supplementary section quantifying both the magnitude and spatial propagation of strain and discuss whether this non-uniformity introduces site-to-site variations, particularly relevant for studies involving inter-site coupling or energy landscapes.
3. The manuscript notes that reduced wavevector resolution and mild aberrations arise when employing a single low-magnification Bertrand lens, yet the implications are only discussed qualitatively. For a technology that aims to simplify high-NA spectroscopy, a quantitative assessment is essential. The authors should provide a clear comparison of achievable k-space resolution or distortion metrics for different optical configurations. A concise table or figure illustrating trade-offs between magnification, NA, and resolution would make the setup’s performance limits and cost–benefit decisions more transparent to potential users.
4. The study demonstrates parallel k-space imaging across multiple sites but does not yet showcase the platform’s potential for exploring dynamic or collective effects. The presented data primarily reflect independent site responses without evidence of spatial coupling, relaxation, or cross-talk. Since one of the main claims is enabling multiplexed studies of interacting systems, the inclusion of preliminary results or discussions highlighting site-to-site dynamics or inter-site correlations would substantially strengthen the manuscript’s impact.
5. The observed reduction in condensation threshold highlights improved excitation efficiency through the microlenses, yet it remains unclear whether the lens shape was optimized specifically for excitation focusing quality or simply derived from detection optimization criteria. The authors should clarify if ray-tracing simulations incorporated parameters such as optical spot size, field uniformity, and intensity profile relevant to excitation. This would establish whether the threshold reduction stems from deliberate excitation design or incidental high-NA performance.
6. Several essential fabrication and design details are distributed through the Supplementary Information (e.g., Fig. S5, S10, Table I), but the main text references are inconsistent. To ensure reproducibility and clarity, the authors should verify that all critical parameters, including microlens dimensions, array spacing, and refractive index profiles, are clearly compiled and cross-referenced. A single summary table consolidating these parameters would be valuable for readers intending to replicate the fabrication process.
Overall, the work delivers a methodological advance in cryogenic, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The concept of an integrated microlens array as a miniature optical instrument replacing a conventional high-NA objective is both elegant and impactful. However, to fully establish the approach as a reliable reference for future users, the authors should better quantify fabrication-induced perturbations and performance trade-offs.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript presented by M. Furman et al. introduces a compact and scalable method for angle-resolved spectroscopy using arrays of 3D-printed microlenses integrated onto semiconductor microcavities. Each microlens enables high-resolution momentum-space imaging without the need for bulky optics, even under cryogenic conditions. The authors demonstrate the capabilities of the technique for both passive microcavities and exciton-polariton studies. They show that the method allows access to larger wavevector values, enables multiplexing of different points in the real-space image, and can reduce exciton-polariton condensation thresholds.
I have found the reuslts very interesting and creative. The fabrication strategy is well explained, and the characterization is rigorous, including comparisons with theoretical models that support the effectiveness of the technique. I find the paper scientifically sound, with a well-supported hypothesis and appropriate references. The novelty of the work is clearly established in comparison with existing literature even if perhaps the versatilty of th technique in comparison with the literature introduced by the authors can be a bit overrated in the text.
I believe some clarifications are needed—particularly a clearer explanation of the measurement technique—before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Below, I provide my detailed comments to the authors.
General comment:
1. I generally missed a more in-depth discussion on how the presence of the microlens might affect the actual photonic response of the photonic structure under consideration. The authors mention local strain on page 3, paragraph 11, as a source of a blue shift in the exciton energies, but there are no comments on the effect of the microlens on the overall cavity response for samples A, B, or C.
For instance, in the case of Sample A, if the top layer is SiO₂ and a microlens layer with a similar refractive index is fabricated on top (as it is the case), one would expect the reflectance of the top mirror—and therefore the cavity response—to change as well. Should the cavity designs be reconsidered to account for this?ç
2.
In the same vein, the authors mention in the conclusions that this system could be suitable for waveguides or 2D material photonics. From the evidence presented, it is clear that the technique works very well for planar samples, but it is difficult for me to foresee how this could be applied to in-plane nanostructured samples without affecting the actual response of the nanostructure itself. It would be helpful if the authors could include a few comments in that direction to clarify the actual effect of the microlens on the photonic response of the sample.
3. The manuscript relies heavily on the comparison between two illumination/collection strategies: the standard objective lens and the microlens, in both cases combined with a Bertrand lens. However, the diagram that actually illustrates the optical differences between these approaches is only shown in Supplementary Information (SI Fig. S5). This figure needs to be revisited frequently to follow the discussions throughout the manuscript. In my opinion, this figure—or a similar one—should be included in the main text, possibly as part of Fig. 1, due to its importance for understanding the experimental setup and results. Figures 1a and 1b are effective in showing the angular limitations of the objective lens, but they may be misleading regarding the technique, as the Bertrand lens is missing in both cases. Including it would help clarify that the plane analyzed to obtain the dispersion in each scenario is the Fourier plane of the objective lens and the microlens, respectively.
4. Overall, I have missed any comment or analysis regarding the polarization. Especially considering that the dispersion of optical microcavities like the ones presented here will have a strong dependence on polarization (TE or TM) at large wavevectors. Please include in the text whether the characterization has been performed under polarization-selective conditions and whether this can affect the measurements.
Specific comments:
1. Fig. 1e–f and Related Discussion:
The comparison between the standard approach using an objective lens and the proposed microlens approach appears to show that the cavity exhibits a lower Q-factor when measured with the microlens (Fig. 1f and g). While the discussion effectively addresses the dispersion, which fits the experimental data obtained with the microlens quite well, I believe a comment on the noticeable differences in the FWHM of the cavity dip between the two cases would be appropriate here.
Is the lower Q observed in the microlens measurements due to the reduced momentum-space resolution, as mentioned later in the context of the photoluminescence experiments? Or is it instead related to modifications in the overall photonic system response of the cavity caused by the presence of the microlens?
2. Fig. 1 – Reflectance Characterization with White Light:

Key results
The authors have performed a study on the performance of microlens arrays, made via 2-photon lithography, fabricated directly on microcavity structures as a means to produce high-k dispersion plots. These arrays are of particular interest in scenarios where high NA objective lenses, with their low working distance requirements, are not appropriate or feasible to use.
To show the breadth and applicability of this approach, three different optical phenomena are analysed via light collected using the microlens array system; a room-temperature bare cavity characterisation, a GaAs cavity that demonstrates strong coupling at cryogenic temperatures and a CdTe microcavity that exhibits Bose Einstein condensation. It is for scenarios akin to the 2nd and 3rd experiment where the microlens technique seems to be particularly effective; for room temperature measurements the system is comparable to traditional optical lenses (as demonstrated by the authors), but in systems requiring the use of a cryostat the physical limitations of temperature and space mean that the high-NA objective lenses required are no longer applicable, offering a real benefit of using the microlens array instead.
In addition to this, the array of microlenses also offers a route to parallelising or multiplexing measurements, where the light from each lens in the array can be analysed individually as part of the collective. This also offers advantages over single conventional objective lenses, and the authors present several scenarios where this approach will either improve upon, or even not be possible, Fourier plane objective lens measurement approaches.
The paper is more a demonstration of the capabilities of the proposed and demonstrated system than an explanation of the physical phenomena measured. Having said that, the data presented from each of the 3 measurement approaches are clear and well presented, with good correspondence to any modelled data. Where there are small discrepancies, sensible explanations are provided, such as the fabrication induced strain resulting in small blue shifts to the collected data in the strong coupling section. I think the data collected is clear and supports the central message of the paper.
Significance
I think for some specific cases, as given by the authors, this method will offer a real opportunity to make high-k measurements of samples where that would be otherwise very challenging. There are many scenarios I can envision where adding microlenses would not work, or would be actively detrimental to the samples, but there are enough circumstances where this approach would be advantageous that I think it would be of use to the field to publish this work.
Data and methodology
The data presented is clear and well explained. Given the nature of this paper, it was very important that the methodology is clear and well explained. Apart for some clarification I think is needed, and outlined below, I think the authors have presented their method well and in a fashion that would allow others to replicate this work or to adapt it for their own research purposes.
Analytical approach
The analysis of the experimental data, and the comparisons to modelled data, are more than appropriate for the work. The supplementary information provides significant details for the models and simulations used.
Clarity and context
I have no concerns about the clarity or context of the work, I enjoyed reading the paper and all the language used is clear and appropriate.
Suggested improvements
Overall, I think this is an interesting method that opens up a lot of possibilities for otherwise challenging or impossible high-k measurements. I think there are a couple of areas that need slightly clarifying or expanding (see list below) but with those areas covered I would be happy to recommend publishing this work.
• I appreciate that the quantum well systems are not the purpose of this paper, but if anyone wanted to replicate this work I don’t think they could do as it stands due to the lack of details on their fabrication. Please could you add further details on their fabrication and what substrate the system is fabricated on. Even a reference to a paper detailing their fabrication process would be welcome.
• From the images of the microlens array, it is clear there is some inhomogeneity to the lens fabrication; some appear slightly different sizes or different shapes. Have you performed any analysis of the structure of the arrays, to give a range of errors on the lens size, for instance?
Given the detailed beam propagation work in the SI, it is clear that small deviations from the desired shape can have quite a significant role. Your simultaneous imaging work seems to show that the arrays you have fabricated do not exhibit significant problems from the structural inhomogeneity, but there will be a limit to how far that can be Please could you include some analysis of the inhomogenity of the structures in the methods section or SI.
•In figure 2, and also in figure 10c, there appears to be an extra mode with a fairly flat dispersion, which isn’t accounted for by the model. Do you have an idea of the origin of this mode, or an account of why it appears experimentally but not in the model? A comment in the paper on its origins would be appropriate, but I don’t think it would in any way negate your interpretation.

### Reviewer 1

Furman et al. present an integration of 3D-printed ellipsoidal microlens arrays directly onto optical microcavities for multiplexed, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The approach successfully replaces bulky microscope objectives with integrated on-chip optics, achieving broad numerical aperture access (up to NA ≈ 0.95) even under cryogenic conditions. The demonstration of 64-site simultaneous k-space imaging represents a genuine breakthrough in experimental methodology. However, a number of conceptual and technical aspects require clarification. These include a fuller quantification of strain-induced effects, explicit comparison of wavevector resolution trade-offs, and a stronger substantiation of the claimed dynamic multiplexing capabilities.
Below are some comments for the author’s consideration.
1. The 3D-printed polymer microlenses introduce localized strain on the semiconductor surface, leading to measurable blueshifts of the exciton and cavity resonances. Given that this strain can affect local mode energies and potentially distort comparisons across the microlens array, its influence requires deeper quantification. The current acknowledgment of this effect in the text is insufficient for reproducibility. The authors should include a supplementary section quantifying both the magnitude and spatial propagation of strain and discuss whether this non-uniformity introduces site-to-site variations, particularly relevant for studies involving inter-site coupling or energy landscapes.
3. The manuscript notes that reduced wavevector resolution and mild aberrations arise when employing a single low-magnification Bertrand lens, yet the implications are only discussed qualitatively. For a technology that aims to simplify high-NA spectroscopy, a quantitative assessment is essential. The authors should provide a clear comparison of achievable k-space resolution or distortion metrics for different optical configurations. A concise table or figure illustrating trade-offs between magnification, NA, and resolution would make the setup’s performance limits and cost–benefit decisions more transparent to potential users.
4. The study demonstrates parallel k-space imaging across multiple sites but does not yet showcase the platform’s potential for exploring dynamic or collective effects. The presented data primarily reflect independent site responses without evidence of spatial coupling, relaxation, or cross-talk. Since one of the main claims is enabling multiplexed studies of interacting systems, the inclusion of preliminary results or discussions highlighting site-to-site dynamics or inter-site correlations would substantially strengthen the manuscript’s impact.
5. The observed reduction in condensation threshold highlights improved excitation efficiency through the microlenses, yet it remains unclear whether the lens shape was optimized specifically for excitation focusing quality or simply derived from detection optimization criteria. The authors should clarify if ray-tracing simulations incorporated parameters such as optical spot size, field uniformity, and intensity profile relevant to excitation. This would establish whether the threshold reduction stems from deliberate excitation design or incidental high-NA performance.
6. Several essential fabrication and design details are distributed through the Supplementary Information (e.g., Fig. S5, S10, Table I), but the main text references are inconsistent. To ensure reproducibility and clarity, the authors should verify that all critical parameters, including microlens dimensions, array spacing, and refractive index profiles, are clearly compiled and cross-referenced. A single summary table consolidating these parameters would be valuable for readers intending to replicate the fabrication process.
Overall, the work delivers a methodological advance in cryogenic, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The concept of an integrated microlens array as a miniature optical instrument replacing a conventional high-NA objective is both elegant and impactful. However, to fully establish the approach as a reliable reference for future users, the authors should better quantify fabrication-induced perturbations and performance trade-offs.

Key results
The authors have performed a study on the performance of microlens arrays, made via 2-photon lithography, fabricated directly on microcavity structures as a means to produce high-k dispersion plots. To show the breadth and applicability of this approach, three different optical phenomena are analysed via light collected using the microlens array system; a room-temperature bare cavity characterisation, a GaAs cavity that demonstrates strong coupling at cryogenic temperatures and a CdTe microcavity that exhibits Bose Einstein condensation. It is for scenarios akin to the 2nd and 3rd experiment where the microlens technique seems to be particularly effective; for room temperature measurements the system is comparable to traditional optical lenses (as demonstrated by the authors), but in systems requiring the use of a cryostat the physical limitations of temperature and space mean that the high-NA objective lenses required are no longer applicable, offering a real benefit of using the microlens array instead.

This also offers advantages over single conventional objective lenses, and the authors present several scenarios where this approach will either improve upon, or even not be possible, Fourier plane objective lens measurement approaches.

## Introduction

Inparticular,three-dimensionalprintingofmicroopticalcomponentsprovides remarkable freedom to design monolithic architectureswithsite-specificfunctionality.

In nanophotonics and plasmonics, the directionalityoflightpropagationplaysanessentialrole. On the fundamental level, BFP imaging allows to determine the direction of a dipole transition, such as identifying the orientation of single molecules17,18 or carbonnanotubes19.Thesamemethodhasbeenusedto distinguishthein-planeorout-of-planecharacterofexcitonsinlayeredmaterials20,21, theirheterostructures22 andthinorganicfilmsinOLEDs23.Italsoallowstodifferentiate from the most common electric-dipole transitions scarce magnetic-dipole ones, occurring in rare earthscomplexes24orin2Dperovskites25.

In systems such as photonic crystals, nanostructures, metasurfaces, or optical cavities, the wavelength and wavevector of photons are connected, forming intricate energy-momentum dispersion relations. There, momentum-resolved spectroscopy enables the experimental study of a wide range of physical phenomena originating from the specific structure in momentum-space. Conventional approaches to reciprocal space imaging rely on high-magnification, high-numerical-aperture(NA)microscopeobjectivestoaccessabroad angle range, often spanning several tens of degrees. ## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

Furman et al. present an integration of 3D-printed ellipsoidal microlens arrays directly onto optical microcavities for multiplexed, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The approach successfully replaces bulky microscope objectives with integrated on-chip optics, achieving broad numerical aperture access (up to NA ≈ 0.95) even under cryogenic conditions. The demonstration of 64-site simultaneous k-space imaging represents a genuine breakthrough in experimental methodology. However, a number of conceptual and technical aspects require clarification. These include a fuller quantification of strain-induced effects, explicit comparison of wavevector resolution trade-offs, and a stronger substantiation of the claimed dynamic multiplexing capabilities.
Below are some comments for the author’s consideration.
1. The 3D-printed polymer microlenses introduce localized strain on the semiconductor surface, leading to measurable blueshifts of the exciton and cavity resonances. Given that this strain can affect local mode energies and potentially distort comparisons across the microlens array, its influence requires deeper quantification. The current acknowledgment of this effect in the text is insufficient for reproducibility. The authors should include a supplementary section quantifying both the magnitude and spatial propagation of strain and discuss whether this non-uniformity introduces site-to-site variations, particularly relevant for studies involving inter-site coupling or energy landscapes.
3. The manuscript notes that reduced wavevector resolution and mild aberrations arise when employing a single low-magnification Bertrand lens, yet the implications are only discussed qualitatively. For a technology that aims to simplify high-NA spectroscopy, a quantitative assessment is essential. The authors should provide a clear comparison of achievable k-space resolution or distortion metrics for different optical configurations. A concise table or figure illustrating trade-offs between magnification, NA, and resolution would make the setup’s performance limits and cost–benefit decisions more transparent to potential users.
4. The study demonstrates parallel k-space imaging across multiple sites but does not yet showcase the platform’s potential for exploring dynamic or collective effects. The presented data primarily reflect independent site responses without evidence of spatial coupling, relaxation, or cross-talk. Since one of the main claims is enabling multiplexed studies of interacting systems, the inclusion of preliminary results or discussions highlighting site-to-site dynamics or inter-site correlations would substantially strengthen the manuscript’s impact.
5. The observed reduction in condensation threshold highlights improved excitation efficiency through the microlenses, yet it remains unclear whether the lens shape was optimized specifically for excitation focusing quality or simply derived from detection optimization criteria. The authors should clarify if ray-tracing simulations incorporated parameters such as optical spot size, field uniformity, and intensity profile relevant to excitation. This would establish whether the threshold reduction stems from deliberate excitation design or incidental high-NA performance.
6. Several essential fabrication and design details are distributed through the Supplementary Information (e.g., Fig. S5, S10, Table I), but the main text references are inconsistent. To ensure reproducibility and clarity, the authors should verify that all critical parameters, including microlens dimensions, array spacing, and refractive index profiles, are clearly compiled and cross-referenced. A single summary table consolidating these parameters would be valuable for readers intending to replicate the fabrication process.
Overall, the work delivers a methodological advance in cryogenic, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The concept of an integrated microlens array as a miniature optical instrument replacing a conventional high-NA objective is both elegant and impactful. However, to fully establish the approach as a reliable reference for future users, the authors should better quantify fabrication-induced perturbations and performance trade-offs.

### Reviewer 3

Key results
The authors have performed a study on the performance of microlens arrays, made via 2-photon lithography, fabricated directly on microcavity structures as a means to produce high-k dispersion plots. These arrays are of particular interest in scenarios where high NA objective lenses, with their low working distance requirements, are not appropriate or feasible to use.
To show the breadth and applicability of this approach, three different optical phenomena are analysed via light collected using the microlens array system; a room-temperature bare cavity characterisation, a GaAs cavity that demonstrates strong coupling at cryogenic temperatures and a CdTe microcavity that exhibits Bose Einstein condensation. It is for scenarios akin to the 2nd and 3rd experiment where the microlens technique seems to be particularly effective; for room temperature measurements the system is comparable to traditional optical lenses (as demonstrated by the authors), but in systems requiring the use of a cryostat the physical limitations of temperature and space mean that the high-NA objective lenses required are no longer applicable, offering a real benefit of using the microlens array instead.
In addition to this, the array of microlenses also offers a route to parallelising or multiplexing measurements, where the light from each lens in the array can be analysed individually as part of the collective. This also offers advantages over single conventional objective lenses, and the authors present several scenarios where this approach will either improve upon, or even not be possible, Fourier plane objective lens measurement approaches.
The paper is more a demonstration of the capabilities of the proposed and demonstrated system than an explanation of the physical phenomena measured. Having said that, the data presented from each of the 3 measurement approaches are clear and well presented, with good correspondence to any modelled data. Where there are small discrepancies, sensible explanations are provided, such as the fabrication induced strain resulting in small blue shifts to the collected data in the strong coupling section. I think the data collected is clear and supports the central message of the paper.
Significance
I think for some specific cases, as given by the authors, this method will offer a real opportunity to make high-k measurements of samples where that would be otherwise very challenging. There are many scenarios I can envision where adding microlenses would not work, or would be actively detrimental to the samples, but there are enough circumstances where this approach would be advantageous that I think it would be of use to the field to publish this work.
Data and methodology
The data presented is clear and well explained. Given the nature of this paper, it was very important that the methodology is clear and well explained. Apart for some clarification I think is needed, and outlined below, I think the authors have presented their method well and in a fashion that would allow others to replicate this work or to adapt it for their own research purposes.
Analytical approach
The analysis of the experimental data, and the comparisons to modelled data, are more than appropriate for the work. The supplementary information provides significant details for the models and simulations used.
Clarity and context
I have no concerns about the clarity or context of the work, I enjoyed reading the paper and all the language used is clear and appropriate.
Suggested improvements

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Furman et al. present an integration of 3D-printed ellipsoidal microlens arrays directly onto optical microcavities for multiplexed, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The approach successfully replaces bulky microscope objectives with integrated on-chip optics, achieving broad numerical aperture access (up to NA ≈ 0.95) even under cryogenic conditions. The demonstration of 64-site simultaneous k-space imaging represents a genuine breakthrough in experimental methodology. However, a number of conceptual and technical aspects require clarification. These include a fuller quantification of strain-induced effects, explicit comparison of wavevector resolution trade-offs, and a stronger substantiation of the claimed dynamic multiplexing capabilities.
Below are some comments for the author’s consideration.
1. The 3D-printed polymer microlenses introduce localized strain on the semiconductor surface, leading to measurable blueshifts of the exciton and cavity resonances. Given that this strain can affect local mode energies and potentially distort comparisons across the microlens array, its influence requires deeper quantification. The current acknowledgment of this effect in the text is insufficient for reproducibility. The authors should include a supplementary section quantifying both the magnitude and spatial propagation of strain and discuss whether this non-uniformity introduces site-to-site variations, particularly relevant for studies involving inter-site coupling or energy landscapes.
3. The manuscript notes that reduced wavevector resolution and mild aberrations arise when employing a single low-magnification Bertrand lens, yet the implications are only discussed qualitatively. For a technology that aims to simplify high-NA spectroscopy, a quantitative assessment is essential. The authors should provide a clear comparison of achievable k-space resolution or distortion metrics for different optical configurations. A concise table or figure illustrating trade-offs between magnification, NA, and resolution would make the setup’s performance limits and cost–benefit decisions more transparent to potential users.
4. The study demonstrates parallel k-space imaging across multiple sites but does not yet showcase the platform’s potential for exploring dynamic or collective effects. The presented data primarily reflect independent site responses without evidence of spatial coupling, relaxation, or cross-talk. Since one of the main claims is enabling multiplexed studies of interacting systems, the inclusion of preliminary results or discussions highlighting site-to-site dynamics or inter-site correlations would substantially strengthen the manuscript’s impact.
5. The observed reduction in condensation threshold highlights improved excitation efficiency through the microlenses, yet it remains unclear whether the lens shape was optimized specifically for excitation focusing quality or simply derived from detection optimization criteria. The authors should clarify if ray-tracing simulations incorporated parameters such as optical spot size, field uniformity, and intensity profile relevant to excitation. This would establish whether the threshold reduction stems from deliberate excitation design or incidental high-NA performance.
6. Several essential fabrication and design details are distributed through the Supplementary Information (e.g., Fig. S5, S10, Table I), but the main text references are inconsistent. To ensure reproducibility and clarity, the authors should verify that all critical parameters, including microlens dimensions, array spacing, and refractive index profiles, are clearly compiled and cross-referenced. A single summary table consolidating these parameters would be valuable for readers intending to replicate the fabrication process.
Overall, the work delivers a methodological advance in cryogenic, angle-resolved spectroscopy. The concept of an integrated microlens array as a miniature optical instrument replacing a conventional high-NA objective is both elegant and impactful. However, to fully establish the approach as a reliable reference for future users, the authors should better quantify fabrication-induced perturbations and performance trade-offs.

### Reviewer 3

Key results
The authors have performed a study on the performance of microlens arrays, made via 2-photon lithography, fabricated directly on microcavity structures as a means to produce high-k dispersion plots. These arrays are of particular interest in scenarios where high NA objective lenses, with their low working distance requirements, are not appropriate or feasible to use.
To show the breadth and applicability of this approach, three different optical phenomena are analysed via light collected using the microlens array system; a room-temperature bare cavity characterisation, a GaAs cavity that demonstrates strong coupling at cryogenic temperatures and a CdTe microcavity that exhibits Bose Einstein condensation. It is for scenarios akin to the 2nd and 3rd experiment where the microlens technique seems to be particularly effective; for room temperature measurements the system is comparable to traditional optical lenses (as demonstrated by the authors), but in systems requiring the use of a cryostat the physical limitations of temperature and space mean that the high-NA objective lenses required are no longer applicable, offering a real benefit of using the microlens array instead.
In addition to this, the array of microlenses also offers a route to parallelising or multiplexing measurements, where the light from each lens in the array can be analysed individually as part of the collective. This also offers advantages over single conventional objective lenses, and the authors present several scenarios where this approach will either improve upon, or even not be possible, Fourier plane objective lens measurement approaches.
The paper is more a demonstration of the capabilities of the proposed and demonstrated system than an explanation of the physical phenomena measured. Having said that, the data presented from each of the 3 measurement approaches are clear and well presented, with good correspondence to any modelled data. Where there are small discrepancies, sensible explanations are provided, such as the fabrication induced strain resulting in small blue shifts to the collected data in the strong coupling section. I think the data collected is clear and supports the central message of the paper.
Significance
I think for some specific cases, as given by the authors, this method will offer a real opportunity to make high-k measurements of samples where that would be otherwise very challenging. There are many scenarios I can envision where adding microlenses would not work, or would be actively detrimental to the samples, but there are enough circumstances where this approach would be advantageous that I think it would be of use to the field to publish this work.
Data and methodology
The data presented is clear and well explained. Given the nature of this paper, it was very important that the methodology is clear and well explained. Apart for some clarification I think is needed, and outlined below, I think the authors have presented their method well and in a fashion that would allow others to replicate this work or to adapt it for their own research purposes.
Analytical approach
The analysis of the experimental data, and the comparisons to modelled data, are more than appropriate for the work. The supplementary information provides significant details for the models and simulations used.
Clarity and context
I have no concerns about the clarity or context of the work, I enjoyed reading the paper and all the language used is clear and appropriate.
Suggested improvements
Overall, I think this is an interesting method that opens up a lot of possibilities for otherwise challenging or impossible high-k measurements. I think there are a couple of areas that need slightly clarifying or expanding (see list below) but with those areas covered I would be happy to recommend publishing this work.
• I appreciate that the quantum well systems are not the purpose of this paper, but if anyone wanted to replicate this work I don’t think they could do as it stands due to the lack of details on their fabrication. Please could you add further details on their fabrication and what substrate the system is fabricated on. Even a reference to a paper detailing their fabrication process would be welcome.
• From the images of the microlens array, it is clear there is some inhomogeneity to the lens fabrication; some appear slightly different sizes or different shapes. Have you performed any analysis of the structure of the arrays, to give a range of errors on the lens size, for instance?
Given the detailed beam propagation work in the SI, it is clear that small deviations from the desired shape can have quite a significant role. Your simultaneous imaging work seems to show that the arrays you have fabricated do not exhibit significant problems from the structural inhomogeneity, but there will be a limit to how far that can be Please could you include some analysis of the inhomogenity of the structures in the methods section or SI.
•In figure 2, and also in figure 10c, there appears to be an extra mode with a fairly flat dispersion, which isn’t accounted for by the model. Do you have an idea of the origin of this mode, or an account of why it appears experimentally but not in the model? A comment in the paper on its origins would be appropriate, but I don’t think it would in any way negate your interpretation.
